printed_headline_estimate: CWS reform vs matched IWS wards (SES-adjusted OLS, Table 4, PDF p. 7 / p. 126): Ongoing water expenditures = +111.679*** Rs/month (SE = 11.385, p < 0.01, N = 2,739; unadjusted CWS mean 204 [95% CI: 186.6–220.3] vs IWS 96 [95% CI: 81.9–111.2], Table 3); Amortized storage/coping investment = -133.644*** Rs/month (SE = 4.875, p < 0.01, N = 3,453; CWS 115 [95% CI: 109.6–120.4] vs IWS 251 [95% CI: 240.8–261.2]); Total monetary water costs = –32.633*** Rs/month (SE = 12.330, p < 0.01, N = 2,688; CWS 310 [95% CI: 292.5–327.5] vs IWS 354 [95% CI: 334.3–374.2]); Water waiting/management time = –22.632*** hours/month (SE = 0.683, p < 0.01, N = 3,078; CWS 7.4 [95% CI: 7.1–7.7] vs IWS 29.9 [95% CI: 28.5–31.2]). Affordability (Fig. 4, PDF p. 8): utility bills rose from >1% (IWS) to >3% (CWS) of reported income in bottom two wealth quintiles (non-overlapping 95% CIs; NS in top quintile); billed volumes increased significantly across all quintiles (Fig. 5). Secondary Family A covariate in Table 4 ('Own their Home'): +23.230* Rs/month on Total Monetary Costs (SE = 14.032, p < 0.10, N = 2,688), +13.173 (SE = 12.911, NS) on Ongoing Expenditures, and +0.193 hours/month (SE = 0.762, NS) on Time.
publication_year_note: Published in World Development, Vol. 109, pp. 121–133 (2018; Accepted 13 April 2018; UC Berkeley eScholarship cover page lists 2018-09-01).
rationale: Using a genetic-matched quasi-experimental cohort of 3,922 enrolled households across 8 continuous water supply (CWS) demonstration wards and 8 intermittent water supply (IWS) control wards in Hubli-Dharwad, India (n = 1,969 CWS; n = 1,953 IWS), the paper reports 95% confidence intervals (Table 3, Figs. 2–5) and SES-adjusted OLS regressions (Table 4, N = 2,688 to 3,453) evaluating the KUWASIP municipal water system reform. Under KUWASIP (Family C: tariffs/administrative-structure/utility reform), all household connections were mandatorily registered with the utility, metered with a Rs 30/month meter fee plus an increasing-block volumetric tariff (replacing Rs 90 flat-rate / subsidized tariffs; Table 2), free public standpipes and borewells were decommissioned to eliminate non-revenue water, and pipes were upgraded to 24x7 continuous supply. The reform nearly doubled monthly ongoing water bill expenditures (+111.679*** Rs/month, p < 0.01) and significantly raised water bills as a share of income from >1% to >3% in the two poorest wealth quintiles (affordability outcome), while reducing total monthly monetary water costs once amortized storage investments are included (–32.633*** Rs/month, p < 0.01), cutting household waiting/collection time (–22.632*** hours/month, p < 0.01), and increasing billed water consumption across all quintiles. Confidence is set to medium because the CWS treatment indicator bundles the tariff, metering, registration, and public-tap-closure rules with physical pipe replacement and 24x7 hydraulic pressurization (the authors note they cannot separate tariff increases from higher consumption in the bill increase). Table 4 also reports inferential OLS estimates for household tenure ('Own their Home', Family A) on water expenditures and collection time.
